messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Salesperson
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 40

He is 29, European, single, and works in sales, a job that depends on being alert, persuasive, and able to recover quickly from rejection. Before the storm, he prides himself on being adaptable. He is the kind of person who keeps a polished schedule, returns calls promptly, and likes to think he can handle pressure better than most people. That sense of himself changes the night the natural disaster comes through his town.

It begins as weather on a screen, one of those local forecasts that people half-watch while making dinner or scrolling their phones. He is at home alone after work, tired from a day of client meetings and follow-up calls, when the alerts start escalating. He remembers standing in his apartment, phone in hand, reading the warning repeatedly while telling himself he has seen storms before. By the time the wind rises hard enough to shake the windows, he is already tense but still trying to stay logical. He moves from room to room, checking doors, gathering a flashlight, charging his phone, and listening for updates. When the power fails, the apartment becomes strangely quiet except for the sound of wind and debris striking the building.

What follows stays with him in fragments: the cracking noise overhead, the sudden vibration of the floor, the sharp smell of wet insulation and dust, the panic of realizing he is not as in control as he believed. He spends the worst of it crouched in a hallway away from the windows, shoulders braced, jaw clenched so hard it aches. He keeps his phone in his hand even though the signal is unreliable, as if holding it can keep him connected to the outside world. Later he says the most frightening part is not knowing whether the noise outside is the storm passing or the building giving way.

In the days after, he moves through the aftermath with a kind of stiff determination. He returns to the apartment to find damage that feels both personal and unreal: broken glass, soaked belongings, ceilings stained with water, the smell of mildew beginning to settle in. He helps a neighbor carry debris down the stairs and checks in on family by phone, telling them he is fine in the same tone he uses with clients when he is trying to close a sale. He stays busy, partly because there is so much to repair and partly because he cannot bear to sit still long enough to feel what happened. At work, he goes back sooner than he should, answering calls with his usual professionalism, but he notices that his concentration slips. A loud knock on the office door makes his chest tighten. Storm warnings on the radio make him mute it immediately.

Over time, the storm starts arriving before the weather does. Dark clouds make his stomach drop. Heavy rain can pull him out of conversation entirely. When wind rattles windows, he scans the room without thinking. At night he checks locks repeatedly and keeps lights on longer than he used to. Sleep is broken by dreams that are not always exact images of the disaster but carry the same feeling of being trapped and unable to get to safety. He wakes sweaty and disoriented, needing a moment to remember where he is. On some mornings he lies still in bed, watching the ceiling, already exhausted by the day ahead.

He notices that he is more irritable than before. Small inconveniences at work—a delayed response from a client, a missed call, traffic on the way to an appointment—feel heavier than they should. He has less patience for social plans and often declines invitations, telling friends he is busy or tired. In truth, he feels flattened by a kind of background dread that makes even ordinary evenings feel effortful. He still performs well enough on the surface, and colleagues likely see him as composed, but he knows how much energy it takes to appear that way.

He also finds himself avoiding reminders in ways that shape his routine. He checks weather apps obsessively, then deletes them and checks again. He takes longer routes when he can, especially if they pass areas that were damaged. He keeps a small emergency kit in his car, a habit that once made him feel prepared and now feels like a talisman against helplessness. He does not talk much about the storm unless asked directly, and even then he tells the story in a controlled, abbreviated way, as if staying concise can keep the memory from opening up.

Since the disaster, he lives with the sense that safety can disappear in an instant. He still goes to work, still dresses neatly, still makes his calls and meets his targets, but there is a watchfulness beneath everything he does. It sits in his body as tension, in his mind as anticipation, and in the quiet moments of his day as a steady, unwanted memory of wind, darkness, and the long hours when he did not know what would happen next.
